results.description: "As per my last email" is just an absolute nightmare phrase, a thing that you hate to see. It's also the title of NOIA's new single, a skittering, thumping, glitched-out avant-club track about the neverending always-online hell of office-job life in our corroded present. With digital effects chopping her voice into shards, NOIA repeats a few phrases again and again: "As per my last email, I haven't been able to focus," "I’m available all night, all day, every day." results.title: Last Call: Verifying the Vintage
results.description: When I first got into guitars, “vintage” wasn’t really a thing. A ’59 Burst was special because our heroes played one. But everything else was just a used guitar. You could score a 1952 Les Paul Gold Top in that greenish gold hue, covered in checking, for a hundred bucks in pawnshops, classifieds, or at garage sales. A buddy of mine had one and was embarrassed every time he pulled it out of its brown case. They just weren’t cool. Luckily, because these old planks were considered second-tier back then, I managed to buy and hold onto a few I couldn’t touch today. As vintage guitars became serious business, authentication usually came down to some old-timer with a good eye and strong opinions. Counterfeiters are getting terrifyingly good. It’s forensics now, not gut feel. So I turned to the pros at Vintage Verified , a third-party guitar analysis lab run by Jon Roncolato and Zach Ziemer, two talented, respected members of Nashville’s guitar community that I’ve known for years. They built out a state-of-the-art lab and hired some of the top chemists in the world, like Dr. Tom Tague Jr., to perform non-destructive scientific testing—spectrometers, analytical chemistry, 3D scanning, the works—to check if a vintage instrument's parts and finish match its claimed era and maker. They examine finish, plastics, hardware, pickups, electronics, body and neck structure, inlays, logos, everything, and compare it against their massive database of known-good and known-suspect examples, and also of period-correct and modern materials alike. I brought them what I believed to be my 1952 Les Paul Standard (refinished with new electronics), my seemingly stock 1954 Les Paul Standard, and my 1956 Les Paul Custom (partially refinished with a neck repair from its misspent ’70s youth). If they’re genuine, the trio could fetch serious money—think north of $80K combined in today’s crazy market. If they’re clever fakes or heavy rebuilds? Maybe $6K–$10K for the lot. "As vintage guitars became serious business, authentication usually came down to some old-timer with a good eye and strong opinions." The anxiety was real. What if I’d been lying to myself all these years? What if my retirement plan was actually worth five percent of what I imagined? I was most concerned about how they could accurately date my 1952 Les Paul. Gibson did not start using the ink-stamped five-digit serial numbers on the back of the headstock until well into 1953. That makes dating a bit of a challenge. On top of that, my ‘52 came to me as a hacked-up husk, having been repeatedly stripped, routed, and repainted over its very rough 72 years on this planet. The Vintage Verified guys told me that if the guitar is a legit 1952, the instrument will likely have at least traces of original paint in the pickup cavities, as it’s very uncommon for someone to strip the concealed guts completely. Cavity remnants in combination with 3D scanning provides a high degree of certainty as to whether a husk is legit or not. The 1952 Gibson Gold Top finish is unique because it used a bronze powder mixed into clear nitrocellulose lacquer instead of modern gold metallic flake or mica. As with most period-correct materials, a period-correct Gibson finish from the 1950s is virtually impossible to recreate. As Vintage Verified put it, the complexity of the chemistry involved in these coatings is far beyond the grasp of many people. But I wonder—when the Boomers finish unloading their collections, will Gen X, Millennials, Gen Z, Alpha, or the incoming Beta crowd even blink? These younger players think nothing of dropping $7 on coffee or $800 on a modeler, but a 70-year-old plank with checking and a questionable neck reset? I’m betting that as the chasm between the Haves, the Have Nots, and the Have Jets grows increasingly larger, the mega rich will run out of things to buy, so they will chase what is rare. You can build as many custom shop reproductions as you want, but unless you have a Delorian and a flux capacitor, you can not build a true ’50s-era Les Paul. I don’t know if I’ll ever sell mine, but at least now I know what I actually own. When I’m gone, there’s objective evidence for my daughter. Maybe she’ll drag them to gigs and bang on them just like she watched me do her whole life. Or maybe she’ll sell them and buy a house. Either way, the guesswork is gone. The process isn’t cheap, but the confidence it gives any future buyer (or inheritor) more than pays for itself. Plus, it just feels good to stop wondering.
